title: An Easy White Bean Pot Pie for Special Nights or Every Night
contentHtml:
A crackly crown of buttered phyllo gives way to creamy white beans and browned mushrooms in thyme-scented gravy—perfect for a weeknight dinner or special occasion like Thanksgiving!

Growing up, a frozen Swanson’s chicken pot pie was a Saturday lunch staple. I’d throw it in the oven when I stopped home between Japanese school and music school, then burn the crap out of my mouth on the creamy mix of carrots, peas, and vaguely chicken-scented protein cubes.

Of course in the years that have followed I’ve made many, many much better chicken pot pies. And while the skyrocketing availability of rotisserie chickens, decent store-bought broth, and frozen pastry has transformed the arduous task of making chicken pot pie from scratch into a relatively simple weeknight process, I sometimes end up asking myself: How much of what makes a chicken pot pie taste like chicken pot pie is actually the chicken?

Certainly not much in those frozen pies. Even in a homemade pie, I’d argue that the essence of a chicken pot pie is the creamy gravy, the scent of thyme of bay leaf, those chunks of vegetables, and the contrast with a shard of buttery crust. That leaves a little wiggle room for the actual chicken. Enough room to wiggle in a couple cans of white beans, even.

For this white bean pie, I start the filling with sliced mushrooms cooked in a bit of oil, letting them cook until the liquid they give off has cooked away and they’ve had a chance to brown lightly. Then I turn down the heat, add some fresh butter, and let some leeks, carrots, and celery soften gently with a few sprigs of thyme and a bay leaf. From there, it’s all pretty standard pot pie procedure: add some flour to form a roux, stir in a mixture of stock and milk and allow it to simmer and thicken. Rather than adding in torn shreds of chicken, instead I add a couple of cans of drained white beans and a big handful of frozen peas.

For the crust, you can easily use store-bought puff pastry, or top the mixture with biscuit dough before baking. In this case, I happened to have frozen phyllo dough, so I went with that. The bottom of the pie was eight layers of phyllo dough laid flat with melted butter brushed between the layers. For the top, rather than making a typical layered crust, I crumpled up and swirled sheets of phyllo and packed them into the baking dish before brushing the entire thing generously with butter.

All of the ridges sticking up get browned and crisp as the pie bakes in the oven, giving you even more of those all-important buttery shards.

This also makes a killer Thanksgiving side or main, especially for the vegetarians in your life!

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • It eats like chicken pot pie but uses even simpler pantry and refrigerator staples.

  • It can serve as a great vegetarian centerpiece for a celebratory meal.

Yield: 6 servings
Active Time: About 40 minutes
Total Time: About 1 hour 30 minutes, plus time to thaw the phyllo

Notes:

  • Cannellini or Great Northern beans both work well, as to garbanzos.

  • The sheet count assumes 9x14-inch phyllo. If yours measures 14x18 inches, cut the stack in half crosswise before counting out the sheets. Thaw according to the package directions.

  • You can use frozen peas and carrots in place of the fresh carrots to make this even easier. Add the frozen peas and carrots when adding the frozen peas in step 3.

Ingredients

For the Filling:

  • 2 tablespoons (30 ml) olive oil

  • 8 ounces (225 g) cremini, white button, shiitake, or mistake mushrooms, cut into bite-sized pieces

  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper

  • 3 tablespoons (45 g) unsalted butter

  • 1 large leek (about 6 oz; 175 g), white and light green parts quartered lengthwise, washed well, and cut into ½-inch pieces

  • 2 medium carrots (about 8 oz; 225 g), cut into roughly ½-inch pieces

  • 2 celery ribs (about 6 oz; 175 g), cut into roughly ½-inch pieces

  • 4 sprigs fresh thyme

  • 1 bay leaf

  • ¼ cup (30 g) all-purpose flour

  • 1 ½ cups (360 ml) low-sodium vegetable or chicken stock

  • 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk

  • Two 15 oz (425 g) cans white beans, drained

  • 1 cup (140 g) frozen peas

For the Crust:

  • 6 tablespoons (85 g) unsalted butter, melted

  • 14 sheets thawed phyllo dough, each about 9x14 inches

Method

  1. Brown the mushrooms. Adjust an oven rack to the lower-middle position and heat the oven to 400°F (205°C). Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the mushrooms and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until their liquid has evaporated and the mushrooms are well browned in spots, 8 to 10 minutes.

  2. Soften the vegetables. Reduce the heat to medium-low and add the butter, leek, carrots, celery, thyme, bay leaf, and another pinch of salt. Cook, stirring occasionally and scraping up the browned bits, until the leek is softened but not browned, about five minutes.

  3. Finish the filling. Sprinkle the flour over the vegetables and cook, stirring, for 1 minute. Combine the stock and milk. Add the liquid all at once and stir to dissolve the flour mixture. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, scraping the bottom and corners of the pan. Cook until the gravy coats the vegetables and thickens to a rich sauce, 3 to 5 minutes. Remove the thyme stems and bay leaf. Fold in the beans and frozen peas, season to taste with salt and pepper, and take the skillet off the heat.

  4. Line the pan. Brush the bottom and sides of a 9x13-inch baking pan with melted butter. Lay a sheet of phyllo in the pan, easing it into the corners, and brush lightly with butter. Repeat with 5 more sheets, staggering them a little so the edges come partway up each side of the pan. Keep the unused phyllo covered with plastic wrap as you work. Spoon in the filling and spread it evenly.

  5. Ruffle the top. Loosely gather one of the remaining sheets lengthwise into a ruffled strip, then curl it into a loose spiral and set it on the filling. Repeat with the remaining 7 sheets, arranging the spirals in two rows of four. Tease the folds apart a little to cover any large gaps. Brush the tops and exposed edges generously with the remaining butter, letting some drip into the folds.

  6. Bake and serve. Bake until the phyllo is deep golden brown, including down in the folds, and the filling is bubbling around the edges, 30 to 35 minutes. Let stand for 10 minutes, then serve with a big spoon.
